text:
Reasoning

1. Count the protons that appear in the ¹H NMR.  
   7.0 ppm (1 H) + 5.5 ppm (1 H) + 2.1 ppm (3 H) + 1.6 ppm (3 H) = 8 hydrogens.

2. Compare with the candidate formulas.  
   • Propenyl acetate (CH₃COO–CH=CH–CH₃) contains 5 carbons and 8 hydrogens (3 H on the acetate-methyl, 3 H on the allylic methyl, and 2 vinylic H).  
   • Butenyl acetate (CH₃COO–CH₂–CH=CH–CH₃) would have 10 observable hydrogens (extra CH₂, 2 H) and should show a signal for an –O–CH₂– group around 4 ppm, which is absent.  
   Therefore the unknown must be a propenyl acetate, not a butenyl acetate.

3. Decide between cis- and trans-propenyl acetate.  
   • The two vinylic protons give a large coupling constant J = 16 Hz (signal at 7.0 ppm is a doublet, J = 16 Hz). A 16 Hz ³Jₕₕ across a C=C bond is characteristic of a trans (E) configuration; cis (Z) alkenes usually show J ≈ 6–12 Hz.  
   • The proton at 5.5 ppm is a doublet of quartets: it is coupled (i) to the trans vinylic proton (J ≈ 16 Hz, giving the doublet) and (ii) to a three-proton methyl group (J ≈ 6–7 Hz, giving the quartet).  
   • The methyl at 1.6 ppm appears as a doublet (coupled to that same vinylic proton, J ≈ 6–7 Hz).  
   • The singlet at 2.1 ppm is the acetate –COCH₃ group.

   This exactly matches the pattern expected for trans-propenyl acetate (CH₃COO–CH=CH–CH₃ with the acetate group and CH₃ group trans to each other).

Conclusion  
The spectrum fits trans-propenyl acetate and rules out the butenyl esters and the cis propenyl isomer.

Answer: B
